title: Buddhism: loving-kindness
hook: may all beings be happy and at ease (Sutta Nipata 1.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, anicca, everything changes. Your line was this too. Day two hundred forty-two.

Think about the way a mother looks at her newborn asleep. Nothing is being asked of that baby. It hasn't earned anything or done anything useful. And the love is total: she'd step in front of a truck for it. Now imagine even a small slice of that toward the person ahead of you in line. Toward the driver who cut you off. Toward every living creature, seen and unseen. It sounds impossible. The Buddha taught that it can be practiced, a little at a time, like a muscle. Today's word: metta.
screen: `A MOTHER AND A SLEEPING BABY.` → `THE PERSON AHEAD OF YOU IN LINE.` → `METTA.`

segments.voice: Metta is Pali, often translated loving-kindness or goodwill. It's related to the word for a friend, so you could also hear it as friendliness: wishing someone well the way a true friend does. The most famous teaching on it is a short text in the Sutta Nipata, one of the oldest parts of the Pali Canon, called the discourse on loving-kindness. Buddhist tradition tells that it was first given to a group of monks who were frightened while meditating in a forest. It begins with character: be capable, upright, gentle, not proud, content with little. Then it opens out into wishing. May all beings be happy and at ease. And it lists them, so no one is left out: weak or strong, tall or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, those already born and those yet to be born. Then comes the picture from the hook. Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Many Buddhists across schools practice metta in meditation, often in a traditional order: first toward yourself, then someone you love, then someone neutral, then someone difficult, and finally all beings everywhere. The phrases are simple and often quiet: may you be well, may you be happy, may you be safe. The idea isn't to fake a feeling. It's to keep pointing the heart in a direction, until the direction becomes a habit.
screen: `METTA: GOODWILL, FRIENDLINESS.` · `SEEN OR UNSEEN, NEAR OR FAR.` · `AS A MOTHER GUARDS HER ONLY CHILD.` · `YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, A FOE.` · then, large: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Wish three people well, the way many Buddhists do: first someone easy to love, then someone neutral, like a neighbor or a cashier, then, if you're willing, someone a little difficult, not the hardest person. To each, inside, offer the traditional wish: may you be well, may you be happy. Then let it spread wider.
Metta. Pali for loving-kindness, friendliness, goodwill: wishing all beings happiness, as a mother guards her only child. Today's word.
Your line: may all beings be well. It's a wish with no one left out. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists chant the Karaniya Metta Sutta and practice metta meditation, offering goodwill in turn to themselves, a loved one, a neutral person, a difficult person and all beings.

chat.says: Is metta about forcing yourself to feel love for everyone?
options: No. It's pointing the heart in a direction, again and again, until it's a habit.
Yes. You keep going until a warm feeling is there for every single person.
No. It's only for people you already love; difficult people are left out.
